translations.text: Philopator received word from those who had returned from the regions from which Antiochus was driving him and his troops out. He gave the signal and ordered all his troops, infantry and cavalry, to march out. Taking his sister Arsinoe with him, he set out and traveled to the territory of Raphia, where Antiochus had arrived and encamped with all his troops.

A man named Theodotus devised a plan. He took a detachment under his command, secretly armed them, and came by night to Ptolemy’s tent, intending to break in and kill him there, and thus settle the war single-handedly. A man named Dositheus, a Jew by birth who had abandoned his ancestral laws, met him and guided him. There in the tent they quickly put an end to [?]. Thus the battle grew fiercer, and matters increasingly favored Antiochus.

Arsinoe immediately rose, crying out with pitiful sobs and her hair let loose. Before the troops she pleaded with them to fight from then on for their own lives and their children. She promised that, if they could find a way to victory, she would give each man two gold necklaces. Thus it happened that the enemy was destroyed at the hands of Antiochus and his troops, with many slaughtered and many led into captivity.

When these plans succeeded and the undertaking was accomplished by his hand, he resolved to visit the cities around him and give them encouragement. He carried this out, distributing gifts at every place of worship and leaving those under his rule encouraged and reassured.

The Hebrews also sent representatives from the people’s council of elders to greet him, present offerings, and express their joy over the victory. He himself resolved to visit them gladly, with affection and joy.

When he arrived in Jerusalem, he presented burnt offerings to the great God with great splendor and many ceremonies, giving thanks and expressing his gratitude. He wished to show still greater devotion at that place. When he reached the holy place, he marveled at the beauty and splendor of the temple and the orderly conduct of its services, and conceived the desire to enter the temple himself.

They stood before him and explained that it was neither lawful nor proper to do this, since even Jews were not permitted to enter, nor were all the priests, but only the high priest—and even he only once each year.

He [?] did not relent at all. Although they brought the laws before him and read them aloud, he still did not relent, but stubbornly insisted on entering. He said, “Even if they are not worthy to enter, I am worthy of this honor.”

“But come now, I ask you: how is it that I enter every other place of worship freely, without restriction, and no one stops me?” Someone else there spoke more boldly, saying, “Why are you so stubborn and persistent? Might there be some reason why it is not proper to enter?” He said, “No! There is no alternative. Whether you wish it or not, I will enter.”

Then the priests, in all their splendid garments, fell down and prostrated themselves, begging God to help them and turn him away from this intention. They filled the temple with cries and tears. The citizens who happened to be there were suddenly alarmed and hurried to that place, whispering about what was happening. Maidens came out of their secluded quarters into the public squares with their mothers. With dust cast upon their hair, they filled the city streets with shrieks and cries.

Even the new brides, who had been sitting adorned in their bridal chambers, forgot their customary modesty and ran boldly through the city streets. Likewise, mothers with newborn children, neglecting the care of their infants, rushed heedlessly through the open grounds, without looking back, and gathered at the greatly honored temple. The prayers of those assembled there multiplied ten thousandfold because the man intended unlawfully to take matters into his own hands and make his way inside. Angered by this, the citizens would not accept such unjust violence from the man.

When they saw that he stood firm and determined to carry out his wishes, they called out to one another and went, each to his own weapons, to arm themselves, equip themselves, prepare to fight, and die for their ancestral customs and the laws of their fathers. They immediately caused a great disturbance there, until the elders of the people could barely calm the crowd and turn those prepared for battle back to the same gatherings for prayer. And the city's crowds returned to those same prayers.

The elders and leading men of the people who were with the king tried to humble his proud thoughts and soften his rebellious obstinacy. But nothing could persuade him; he remained firm and obstinate in carrying out the very wishes he had conceived before.

Likewise, those who were with him, seeing the man's determination, turned again to prayer, begging almighty God to come to their aid, not to despise them or abandon them, and not to surrender their lawful ordinances to be trampled underfoot by arrogant designs. Such were the repeated, heartfelt cries of the assembled crowds, and such an extraordinary clamor arose there, that it seemed not only the people were crying out, but the walls and floors were also resounding. For everyone had resolved to exchange life for death rather than see the holy place turned to defilement.

They began to plead and say: “Lord, Lord, King of heaven and Lord God of all creation, holy among the holy, almighty and all-ruling, look upon our suffering at the hands of this lawless and defiled man, who has grown proud in his audacity.

“You created everything, and you receive everything with gentleness and justice. You are just, Lord, and you judge those who act with pride and arrogance. You destroyed the giants who formerly practiced lawlessness and trusted in their own strength and bravery, bringing upon them the overwhelming force of boundless waters.
“You openly exposed the arrogant people of Sodom to disgrace along with their wicked deeds. You condemned them with fire and sulfur, leaving them as an example of disgrace to later generations.

“You rebuked with various plagues the audacious, violent, and ruthless king Pharaoh, who enslaved your holy people Israel. You displayed your power and showed him the greatness of your might. When he set out in pursuit of your people with many troops, chariots, and horses, you drowned him in the Red Sea.

“But you preserved those who believed in you, making them strong over all creation. When they saw the works of your hands, they blessed you, Lord Almighty. You are the King who created all the boundless and unfathomable heavens, and you chose this city for yourself and sanctified this place for your name—for yourself, who need nothing.”

You gathered this together for the glory of your greatness and the honor of your name. You loved this temple, and you promised the house of Israel that, whatever [?] events might occur or troubles might come upon them, when they came to this holy place with petitions, you would hear our prayers. Now your word is faithful and true.

For many times, when our fathers were oppressed, you helped them in their humiliation and rescued them from great evils. And now, holy King, we too, afflicted because of our many great sins, have been subjected to our enemies, exhausted and bewildered in our weakness. In these days of distress, this impure, proud, and arrogant man seeks a way to slip inside and dishonor the holy place, the temple of the glory of your name, renowned throughout the earth.

Although your dwelling is the heaven of heavens, invisible and beyond the reach of human hands, nevertheless, because you were pleased to dwell in your glory among the splendor of Israel, you sanctified this place. Although we have sinned against you, do not exact vengeance through the defilement brought by the gentiles. Do not let the lawless boast in their pride or rejoice in their arrogant words, saying, ‘We have trampled the holy temple just as the floors of pagan temples are trampled by everyone.’

Wipe away our sins and remove all our offenses. Show your mercy at this present time. Let your mercies come to us quickly, put a blessing in the mouths of us who are ruined and afflicted, and establish peace with us.

But the Holy One who dwells among the holy ones, the all-powerful, almighty God, heard the people's rightful prayers of petition. He struck the man who was still boldly raging against them with great pride and arrogance, drove him violently this way and that, shook him like a reed in the wind, and threw him to the ground on the spot. He lay there fallen, senseless, numb, speechless, and paralyzed, with all his joints loosened, for judgment upon his pride came upon him violently and swiftly.

When his friends and attendants saw that judgment had come upon him so swiftly, they were struck with fear that his life might come to an end. They quickly dragged him outside from within, terrified by those severe blows.

After many hours had passed and the man had regained his senses, he did not repent in his heart after this great punishment. Instead, he began to make still fiercer threats. He ordered preparations for the return journey.

When he reached the land of the Egyptians, he increased the wickedness within himself still further, together with his banquet companions, who had turned away from all justice. Not only was he unsatisfied with his countless abominations, but he reached such boundless audacity that he filled the place with blasphemy. For many of his friends, looking to the king, also followed his wishes.

He put slanders and blasphemies in writing and had them circulated in the public squares. He ordered pillars to be erected around the portico, upon the towers, and an inscription to be affixed, issuing this strict command: ‘If anyone is found who does not offer sacrifice, he must under no circumstances dare to enter the temple. The entire Jewish nation is to be entered in the census among those subject to taxation and servitude under the law. If even a few stubbornly resist, the penalty of death shall be imposed upon them. Those who are not killed shall be branded with fire and made to dance, wearing garlands and holding branches in their hands, at the festival of the gods of Ormazd.’

But so that he might not appear to everyone as an enemy, he also ordered this to be written in the decree: ‘If any of them are willing to adopt the royal laws for themselves, they shall be counted as fellow citizens of the Alexandrians.’

Many of them were shallow-minded and had already been wavering in their former laws. They readily gave themselves over, thinking that they would inherit a great and glorious name if they submitted to the king’s wishes.

Many of them stood firm and resolute in their hearts and did not depart from their holy laws. They offered their treasures in exchange for themselves, so that they might safely escape the register, and remained steadfast in the hope of finding help. They shunned and abhorred those who broke away from them, considering them unclean. They cast them out, separating them from their ancestral laws and the noble estate of holiness.

When the lawless ruler learned of their intentions, he was driven to such furious anger that he ordered them to be brought not only from Jerusalem but from every land where the children of the Hebrews lived. He ordered them to be brought together, gathered, and assembled, and their lives to be wiped from the earth by a cruel death.
When this harsh, bitter, lawless command was issued, they considered the distress of changing their laws worse than the bitterness of death.

But the children of the Hebrews sincerely and uprightly observed the laws in their dealings with the king. They stood firm in the Lord their God and faithfully kept the laws that had been given to them. They separated themselves from the lawlessness of the rebels, and because of this they fell out of favor with many.

Yet their steadfastness in carrying out the observances of the laws won them honor before everyone. Nevertheless, the foreigners took no account of the good deeds of the nation. Instead, they interpreted its worship and dietary laws as opposition and rebellion, saying, “This nation is an enemy both of the king and of the royal forces.” With such slanderous words they brought harm from the king and severe punishment upon them.

But when the Gentiles who were in that city saw the sudden turmoil among the people and the severity of the persecution that had suddenly come upon them, they could neither give any help nor oppose the royal commands.

Nevertheless, they felt pity, comforted and encouraged them, and prayed that the time of wrath would quickly pass. They said, “The Lord their God will not allow such a multitude to be destroyed unjustly.” Others who were their friends, neighbors, and trading partners secretly pledged to help them as far as they could.

But at that time the lawless ruler had become so exalted in his pride that he paid no attention at all to the power of the great God. Instead, he imagined that his authority to carry out his plans would last forever. So he issued letters throughout the whole land in the following form:

“King Antiochus to the commanders, generals, and troops stationed throughout the regions of Egypt: greetings. May you be well. I myself am well in every respect, as are the forces, the government, and the laws.

“You yourselves must have heard about the [?] expedition and with what force I set out, with the help of the gods. It was not through military force, nor through spearheads, nor through the mighty force of bows, but with gentleness and humility and benevolent intentions, to nurture all the regions of Lower Syria and Arabia like a nurse. I acted with every kindness toward everyone.

“We bestowed great honors and gifts upon all the regions of the cities. We came down and arrived at the city of Jerusalem, and we wished to enter the temple, that place of evildoers who never wished to desist from their cunning wickedness.”

On the surface, they welcomed our arrival among them with words, but in their actions they treacherously avoided approaching us. They neither allowed us to approach their temple nor accepted into their temple the visible [?] of our sacrifices. Relying in arrogant pride on what they had possessed since ancient times, they prevented us from entering. They were deprived of the benefits of our benevolent power, which we exercise toward all people.

They wished to display openly the implacable hostility they harbored toward us in their minds, as though they alone among all nations wished to rise in defiance, exercise dominion, reign, grow proud and arrogant, stand tall, and appear stiff-necked toward their benefactors.

When we wished to put our minds at rest concerning their folly, we returned from there to the regions of Egypt with a great victory. We brought all the nations and peoples under our rule with benevolent gentleness and care, as was right and fitting according to our law.

And without harboring resentment against their people for their repeated insolence and audacity, we nevertheless ordered that they be considered worthy of being counted as fellow citizens of the Alexandrians.

But with still worse, perverse designs and deeply rooted treachery, they rejected this benefit for themselves. Since their minds were continually inclined toward evil, they not only rejected the evident honor of this esteemed fellowship, but also abhorred it, despised it, and considered it unclean, both in speech and in silence. They also reject and despise those few who have submitted to us out of affection. They bring urgent distress upon their lives and threaten to bring about the swift destruction of their affairs very soon.

From all this we became convinced of their hostility toward us, and we considered whether, because of their treacherous character, some sudden disturbance might come upon us, and they might, in their lawlessness, grow bold and be found aiding our enemies outside from within. We ordered that, immediately upon receipt of this decree of ours addressed to you, these frenzied evildoers, together with their wives and children, be sent to us with great indignity and hardship, bound by their feet, hands, and necks, surrounded and closely guarded by guards, and subjected to dreadful punishment.

For when these treacherous people suffer punishment and chastisement for their lawless wrongdoing, as their deeds deserve, the ordering of our affairs will be established more peacefully, easily, and securely. But if anyone is found concealing one of them—a man, a woman, or a young child, from advanced old age down to an infant nursing in someone's arms—let that person and his family be put to death with cruel tortures.

But if anyone is found who reports someone lurking in concealment, the goods and possessions of those reported shall become his, and he shall receive a reward from the royal treasury. Honored with the crown of freedom, he shall be summoned to appear in the public squares.

And every place where any of them is discovered lurking in concealment shall be devastated, burned, and left desolate, and shall remain useless for every purpose to people of every nation for all time.

The royal decree was written in this form. In every place where the command of the decree arrived, the pagans gathered from the districts and assembled in the cities, rejoicing with great exultation and gladness. With treacherous deceit they openly unfurled the rancor of their secret designs and boldly displayed their hostility.
And the unbearable grief of the brave men, overflowing with tears, rose in passionate cries and crushed their hearts. The sudden, bitter decree summoned everyone alike to destruction.
For what [?], what city, or indeed any place inhabited by people, or what passage through the streets of all the cities, was not filled with cries of grief, lamentation, and screaming over them?

For with such bitter severity and a merciless decree, they gathered the chosen people from city after city and sent them away through the provincial commanders, to die unjustly outside their homes under the [?] terms of the decree. The anguish and distress amid these unbearable sufferings were so great that even vindictive hearts and envious eyes shed tears out of shared compassion at that pitiful sight of human torment. For suddenly, along the roads of misery—

As they went, they led away the multitude of aged, gray-haired elders, walking with infirm steps, overwhelmed by the weakness of old age. Those who had only just entered marriage with one another, with the still incomplete joy of their newly cherished bridal chambers, were cruelly stripped by the dreadful news and became [?].

And the closely sheltered, veil-covered, [?] brides uncovered their hair when they received the dreadful news. Boldly exposing their oil-perfumed [?], they threw dust on their heads. Instead of songs of joy with companions singing together, they endured the torments of unfamiliar hardship. With their hair loose and disheveled, bound and forcibly dragged through the public squares, they went as far as the ships’ harbors.

And their husbands, with nooses around their bodies instead of youthful rejoicing, their hands bound and driven with goads, cried out in loud weeping over the time that had come upon them. They pictured their fatal end already at their own feet, face to face with Hades.

And so they brought them all in iron bonds, like beasts from the wilderness, bound their necks to the sterns of the ships, and fastened them there with the same chains. They took some of those whose feet and hands were bound and fastened them to the upper, planked deck of the ship. They were numbed and bewildered on every side, so that while the ships were sailing they could not make any move on their own through some trick.

Once they had secured them all aboard the ships in this way, they carried them away and, with a favorable wind, brought them to the appointed place according to the king’s command. They ordered them to be placed outside the city, in the hippodrome, in a spacious, crowded place, to disgrace the people, so that everyone passing back and forth could freely see them. Through this they exacted everyone’s revenge for their former resentment.

When all this had happened, word was again heard that their fellow countrymen were secretly coming out to share their tears over the sudden misery that had befallen their people. When this was reported, the king burst into furious anger. He ordered those who were inside the city to be brought out and mixed with them, and all alike to be subjected to the same punishment, deserving of death. He also ordered the entire people to be recorded by name in a single census register.
For a little before these events became known, out of resentment over their worship, he had ordered that they be destroyed swiftly, all at one time, with severe punishments and great tortures.
And the recording of their census under this bitter, harsh decree of resentment continued relentlessly from sunrise to sunset, dragging on for forty days without reaching completion.

The king, filled with far greater joy than usual, continually ordered all the nobles to offer banquets in the great temple. With his mind led astray from the truth, he honored and praised the lifeless, voiceless, speechless idols with his lawless, impure mouth, and spoke things that were unfitting against the sacred things established by the law.

After the appointed time had passed, the census scribes came and presented the register before the king. They began to plead, declaring it impossible to compile a census of the Jews. “We cannot manage it because of their immeasurable numbers,” they said. “For many are scattered here and there throughout the land and remain uncounted, outside this register. Countless others are in various places and estates throughout the regions of the land of Egypt.”
When the king heard this, he punished the scribes with beatings, as though they had accepted bribes and devised cunning schemes so that they might save the Jews.

They stood by their statement and plainly showed him the exhausted supply of paper and the worn-out pens. All this happened through the help of the Most High, who showed his compassionate care for the Hebrews.

At that time he summoned Hermon, the keeper of the elephants, and sternly ordered him to ready the elephants for the following morning. Without delay he was to prepare them, intoxicated with wine and filled with incense, enraged by frankincense and made savage by unmixed wine, and bring about seven hundred of them into the public square, preparing a terrible punishment for the Hebrew people.

The king gave this command to the keeper of the elephants and returned to his festivities with a large company and the leading nobles, who were even more hostile toward the Hebrew people than the king himself.

When the keeper of the elephants heard the command, he carried it out rigorously and prepared the elephants at once. The other attendants went out and bound the feet and hands of the suffering prisoners. They surrounded them with additional guards to watch through the night, taking every conceivable precaution. In their minds they reckoned that at dawn, in the morning, they would see the final destruction brought upon the people.

The Jews considered themselves powerless on every side and without help, having fallen prey to the Gentiles. With unceasing cries and tears they called upon almighty God, the one who strengthens all powers, the merciful God. Together they fell down and pleaded with him to overturn and reverse the lawless plan and, by a mighty manifestation, avert the death that was already close at hand and had encompassed them hand and foot.
The elephant keeper enraged the merciless beasts, intoxicated with wine and filled with incense, and brought them to the king’s gate at dawn.

But a portion of sleep went forth as a gift from the heavenly, generous, gift-giving God—that beautiful creation allotted from the earliest times as a good share for day and night—and he sent it upon the king. There, by the Lord’s power, he bound the king in a heavy, deep, sweet, pleasant sleep, thwarting him and causing him to stray from his fixed intentions.

Then, when the appointed, deadly hour had passed, the children of the Hebrews praised the holy, heavenly God. Again they fell upon their faces and pleaded with him to complete the gift bestowed by his mighty arm and make it manifest among the proud Gentiles.

When it was about the middle of the tenth hour, all the arrangements for the banquet hall were ready, and the guests were standing in their assigned places. Suddenly someone knocked and announced that the time for the festivities in the banquet hall was nearly passing. The king remembered the time for the festivities and immediately took his seat. He quickly ordered the guests to be called inside and the banquet service to begin. With the cushions prepared, he ordered each man to be brought to his own seat.

He began the festivities and held a feast in the banquet hall, passing the late hours in joy and merriment. When they became absorbed in lengthy rounds of conversation, he summoned the commander of the elephants and rebuked him bitterly and with terrible severity: why or how had the Jews escaped death at the time appointed by his strict command and been found still alive that day?

The commander stood there and explained to him that the royal command had been carried out during the night, and the guests themselves confirmed the commander's words. Then the king restrained the bitterness of his fury and said, “Go your way. Let them have the favor of sleep for this day. But without fail, prepare for tomorrow to bring the elephants, in the same savage state, against the lawless Jewish nation to destroy them.”

When the king said this, everyone, full of joy, praised the command with one voice. Because the hour was late, they parted from one another and went away to their respective lodgings. Yet they did not give themselves over to sleep so much as spend the whole night thinking up schemes for what new torments they might inflict on the suffering people.

As soon as the rooster crowed early in the morning, he prepared the beasts, driving them wild and rousing them with wine and incense. He himself went down into the great hall and walked about there. Meanwhile, the people in the city came pouring out together and gathered, waiting to watch the spectacle of misery that threatened the Jews at dawn that morning.

As hour after hour passed toward their death, the Jews, with many tears, steadfast fasting, and the pitiful sound of lamentation, raised their hands to heaven and begged the great, almighty God to visit them once again and save them from their inescapable death.

[?] The sun's rays spread over the earth, and the king rose and waited for the arrival of the nobles. The commander of the elephants came to the door to show him with his own eyes how the elephants had been roused and made ready.

The king expressed his thanks and marveled at the preparations. Once again, however, he became confused about what was happening and the reason for this lawless haste. Then he changed his mind and threatened the commander of the elephants with punishment because he had not promptly brought the command he had given to completion and shown him the result.

All this happened by the command of the almighty Lord, who turned the firmly established plans for their inescapable death into confusion. Then the commander of the elephants came forward and called the leading nobles as witnesses, showing that the elephants had been roused beforehand, the troops had been prepared, and the royal command had been fully carried out.

Then the king was again filled with great anger because of the greatness of God's compassion, for God wished to frustrate his plans. At that very moment he looked at the commander of the elephants with great anger and severe threats of punishment. He began to speak and said:

Let it be decreed that all fathers, mothers, and children who have come merely to watch be thrown as food to the beasts, and you along with them, in place of these innocent Hebrews, who, from the earliest ancestors down to our forefathers, have preserved righteousness and faithfulness toward us unstained. And if it were not for the affection arising from our being raised together in the same household, I would cut off the sweet sunlight from your eyes and remove you from our midst, you treacherous evildoer.

Thus the elephant keeper suddenly escaped the murderous punishment by a hair’s breadth. His earlier cheerfulness gone, the man withdrew from their midst with a deeply saddened face and [?]. The king’s friends each lowered their heads and ordered the assembled crowd to disperse, each to attend to their own affairs.

When the children of the Hebrews heard the king’s pronouncement, they began to bless the Lord God, the King of kings, all the more, since they had received this further help for themselves. And immediately the king ordered the dinner guests to return to their rejoicing.

He called the master of the elephants again and began speaking to him with severe threats of punishment, saying, “How many times have you been given orders concerning them, you wretch, to arm, equip, and prepare the elephants? At least now have them ready for tomorrow against the murderous, wretched race of the Jews.”

When all the dinner guests heard this, they were still more astonished at the king’s wavering mind. They said, “How long, O king, how long will you put us to the test with these thoughts of yours? You have ordered this impudent race to be exterminated three times, and yet again you revoke your own command. How is it that, because of this, all the cities in their assemblies are more distressed than those evildoers?”

Entirely astray in all this, the king, filled with foolishness, fell into confusion and did not recognize that a visitation from heaven was upon the Hebrews. Again he fiercely swore an oath that would not be fulfilled, saying, “Without any hesitation I will send them to Hades, trampled [?] by the savage beasts. I will muster an army against all Judea, consign its wooden buildings to fire and wash away its clay buildings with water, and carry off as plunder all its goods and possessions and whatever is in it. And I will set fire to their temple, which is kept from us, and make it a house of sacrifices for all time.”

At that time, having heard these words spoken firmly, the dinner guests and his beloved friends of his household, having heard the firmness of his statement, went away rejoicing. They ordered the soldiers to station night guards and trench guards around those confined in the secure place.

The master of the elephants prepared the beasts, rousing them to an uncontrollable frenzy with wine scented and mixed with frankincense. He armed the demon-possessed beasts with terrifying equipment for the next morning, [?] countless corpses fallen there in the arena. Then he came into the hall and urgently pressed the king to slaughter the bound people.

At that time the entire army advanced outside with the formidable beasts. The king intended to see for himself, with pitiless eyes and a merciless heart, the painful destruction of the wretched multitude.

When they arrived at the city gate with the prepared elephants and armed troops, the Jews became aware of the thunder of the troops, the flashing weapons, and the dust that rose and piled up until it reached the clouds. The crowds shouted, and all this surrounding them numbed their minds. They considered this the final end of the misery they had expected. Moved by compassionate pity, fathers and mothers, sons and daughters, sisters and brothers, relatives and beloved friends fell upon one another’s necks, clung to one another, embraced, and kissed one another.

Some took their newborn children in their arms and placed their breasts in the infants’ mouths, reckoning this to be their last feeding. While they stood [?] in the bewilderment of that calamity and in urgent distress, they remembered the earlier help that had come from heaven. Together, with one accord, they drew apart from one another and pulled their breasts away from the little children’s mouths. All together they fell before the divine majesty and rolled about. Raising their voices with loud cries and weeping, they begged the Almighty, the Ruler of all, to turn to them in compassion and, in his great mercy, save those cut off from hope, who had come close to the gates of hell.

A man named Eleazar, distinguished among the priests, advanced in age and adorned and radiant with every virtue and righteousness from childhood, with difficulty calmed the few elders who were with him. Collecting himself, he offered prayers to the holy God and spoke as follows:

“Mighty King, exalted and almighty God, who governs and directs everything, look with your compassionate mercy upon these descendants of Abraham, born of holy Isaac, the sons of Jacob, the allotted portion of your inheritance—a people living as strangers in a foreign land, handed over to destruction.
You are the God who drowned Pharaoh in the sea with his many chariots, horses, and Egyptian troops, consigning him to destruction along with his proud, self-exalting, boastful, and arrogant forces.

You destroyed the countless forces of Sanatruk, king of the Assyrians, in their pomp and boasting. He sought to seize and gather the whole land of Judea under a single sword blade and a single spear point, and grew still more arrogant, advancing against the holy city with a threatening voice, brazen severity, and great insults. You, Lord, struck, broke, and overthrew him, openly demonstrating the strength of your arm to all the nations.

You also saved the three young men in the land of the Babylonians, who willingly surrendered themselves to the fire rather than bow down to objects of vain worship. The fire did not harm even the hair of their heads, and you gave their enemies as food to the power of the fire.
You also brought Daniel out into the light, preserving him unharmed, when through malicious envy he had been thrown into the pit, into the mouths of fearsome beasts.
You also saw the guest of the depths wasting away in the belly of the fish, brought him out unharmed, and set him before his own household.

You, Father, who hates arrogance, loves goodness, and is merciful, the refuge of all, now appear swiftly to this nation of Israelites, who have fallen into the hands of defiled, lawless pagans and are suffering terrible punishment.

But if, because of our impiety, our lives have reached their end in death under these terrors, only save us from the hands of these enemies, and judge us with whatever severe punishment you wish. Do not let the empty-minded, foolishly plotting pagans boast before their vain idols over our destruction and say, ‘Not even their God saved them from our hands.’

But you, who holds all powers, authorities, and dominions forever in your hands, ever-watchful, immortal, merciful God, have mercy and compassion on us. With so much lawless abuse, we bear this unjust and senseless punishment of death and are being sent from life to death like criminals.
May the might of your victory crush and consume the pagans, for your glory has the power to save and deliver this family of Jacob.”

There they fell down and cried out—all the [?], the crowds of children, group after group, and their fathers and mothers—with tears: “Let your mercy be made known to all the nations, that you, our Lord, are with us and have not turned your face away from us. Rather, as you promised before, ‘Even in the land of their enemies I will not let them go from my hands,’ now fulfill that same word of your command, Lord.”

While Eleazar was offering his prayers to God, the king, together with the beasts and his troops, arrived in great anger at the place of the spectacle, the arena. When the children of the Hebrews saw this, they lifted their eyes upward and raised a loud cry to heaven. At the sound of that cry, the mountains and valleys together answered with an echo. An overwhelming disturbance from the two cries came upon the troops.

At that moment the Most High, glorious and greatly honored, the almighty true God, revealed his face. He opened the gates of heaven, from which two fearsome, glorious angels came down, invisible, for they appeared to no one except the Jews.

They struck the enemies in the face, filled the troops with turmoil, and made them full of fear and trembling. They held them all motionless, bound, surrounded, and hemmed in. Even the king’s entire body and bones shook, trembled, and shuddered. The violence of his savage agitation and the fury of his anger dissolved there into bewilderment. The beasts turned back and charged at the armed troops, knocking many of them down and killing them there beneath their feet.

There, the king’s anger quickly turned to pity and tears over his earlier stubborn resolve and harshness. For when he heard the sound of the shouting and considered the destruction of so many, he became angry and burst into tears. Full of anger, he began speaking to his friends and said:

“Go away! Get away! Surely you have become tyrants and want to rule! Despite all my favors, you want to exclude me altogether from deliberations and from sovereignty itself. You have stolen my judgment, you excellent counselors, and by your schemes you have made me do what is of no benefit to our kingdom.

“Who is shaking this mighty, faithful tower, these guardians of our covenants? Who has taken these people from their own homes and is keeping them here, bound, crowded together, and hemmed in like criminal beasts? Who has subjected them to such unlawful, cruel torments and is keeping them bound, surrounded, and hemmed in—people who from the beginning have lived in harmony and righteousness with us, and who, more than all the nations and peoples, have maintained their just loyalty amid many wars and times of turmoil?

“Undo and release these unlawful bonds! Send them back in peace to their own places. Console these children of the almighty, heavenly, living God for the abuse already inflicted, with tenderness and soothing words. From the beginning, in the days of our ancestors, until today, they have given us unhindered rule and secure rights.” In this manner the king plainly expressed his words.

The Hebrews, immediately released from their bonds in the blink of an eye, blessed their almighty Savior, their holy God, having just escaped by a hair’s breadth from the gates of death in an unbelievable way.

After granting this relief to the Hebrews, the king himself returned into the city. He ordered the treasurer to be summoned and said, “Quickly provide wine, [?], and whatever else is needed for a celebration for the Jews for seven days.” For he had commanded them to spend those seven days rejoicing in their deliverance, in the very place where they had expected their own cruel destruction to be carried out.

At that time, as was indicated earlier, they had come in disgrace and reached the point of death—or rather, had already entered the gates of Hades. In place of that bitter doom, they held a joyful banquet at the place of their deliverance, where they had expected destruction and the pit. They arranged seats for feasting in groups and divided into their respective sections, full of joy.

Instead of tearful laments, they took up songs of praise and blessed God, their wonder-working Savior, in their ancestral language. They cast aside weeping and groaning, and began dancing, establishing a sign of joy, peace, and gladness.

Likewise, the king set aside a time for them in the great palace and, with great joy, ordered the guests to be called inside. Looking toward heaven, they continually and repeatedly blessed God above for the people's sudden and marvelous deliverance. Those who had previously handed the people over to destruction, to be torn by beasts and eaten by birds, now rejoiced [?], accepting shame and loss upon themselves. Their fire-breathing anger was quenched, and they celebrated the occasion with gladness.
But the Jews, as we said earlier, formed joyful dances and spent the seven days blessing God with joy and gladness. With unanimous agreement,

they established a rule that these days of rejoicing should be observed in every place where they lived, not for arrogance or gluttony, but in thanksgiving for the deliverance that God had accomplished for them.

They decreed that these days should be included among their annual festivals, and then asked the king to release them to their respective homes. They had been gathered for registration from the twenty-fifth of Pachon until the fourth of Epiphi, forty days.

Furthermore, orders had been issued to put them to death and destroy them at that place from the fifth of Epiphi until the third day of the month [?]. During these days God greatly glorified his mercy and delivered them all unharmed. Thus they rejoiced by the king's command.

For he had ordered that everything needed for the celebration should be provided until the fourteenth day, on which they received the decree for their release. The king himself ordered letters to be sent to every city and every commander, in the following form:

“King Ptolemy Philopator to the commanders and to all the rulers and officials responsible for royal affairs: greetings. Be of good cheer, for we are well, together with our sons, brothers, and all our forces, just as God has prospered our affairs according to our own wishes.

“Now some of our close friends here, acting out of their own malice, approached us with slander and stirred up our minds until they persuaded us to issue an order to gather the entire Jewish people under our authority into one place and slaughter them in an unprecedented spectacle of torture.

And they gave no respite at all, using as a pretext the hostility they had toward all the Gentiles, until they brought them together. They even brought them in chains, with much abuse and torture, treating them as foreigners—or rather, as criminals. Without any questioning or investigation, they were ready to slaughter them all together. For the savagery they displayed was even wilder than that of the rabble and the brutes.

But we punished these people very severely, as is our custom. Yet, because of the kindness we have toward people, we barely spared their lives. And we recognized the heavenly God, for he truly came to the aid of the Jews, as a father would come to the aid of his children.

And again, considering the love and loyalty they had steadfastly maintained toward us, from their ancestors to our ancestors, we ordered their release and pardoned them for all the offenses charged against them. We also ordered that whatever anyone had taken from any of them should be returned to its rightful owner, so that none of them should be deprived of anything at all, and that no one should dare insult them because of these events.

For you must know this: if we choose to deal deceitfully with them or cause them distress, we sin not against a human being, but against God, who rules over all powers and dominions. Such a person will receive retribution not only from a human being, but unfailingly, in every respect, from the Most High. And may you fare well.

When they received that letter, rather than hurrying away immediately, they went in to the king to present a petition and say, “Order that those of this Jewish nation who voluntarily denied the holy God and transgressed God's laws be handed over to us, so that we may inflict on them the punishment required by the laws.” They added, “People who chose to transgress the laws of their ancestors because of the distress of their bellies and their wicked appetite can never act honestly and loyally in the king's affairs.”

The king considered this just and gave them authority to destroy those who had transgressed God's laws wherever they found them throughout the king's dominion, with complete freedom. No one was to oppose them in any way, under threat of royal punishment.

Then they gave thanks and offered blessings, as was the custom of the priests and all the people, and they placed “Hallelujah” at the beginning and end of their words. With rejoicing and gladness, they bowed to the ground and departed from the king.

When they set out on the road, they put to death with torture and public disgrace those of their own nation who had previously transgressed the laws and defiled themselves through lawlessness. On that one day they killed more than three hundred men. They celebrated that day joyfully, because they had seized and captured the defiled and lawless transgressors of their laws and put them to death, while they themselves had found deliverance from the gates of death through God's mercy.

They broke camp, set out, and departed from that city amid all kinds of delights, crowned with flowers of many colors. With joy, rejoicing, and blessings, they gave thanks in sweet voices to the God of their fathers, who is forever the savior of Israel.

When they arrived at the city of Ptolemais, which is called “Rose-bearing” because of the character of the place, the ships in which they had come there had already arrived and were waiting for them. By common agreement they spent seven days there. They were joyful, because the king had ordered that abundant provisions be prepared for their journey until they reached their respective homes.

And when they reached the place, they gave thanks as befitted the gifts they had received. They also established a law to include those days among their annual festivals and celebrate them with joy. They presented offerings, set up monuments at the places of rejoicing, and included that day among their annual festivals.

They gathered in one place, offered prayers, and gave thanks. They parted from one another alive and unharmed, freed, confident, joyful, and saved. By sea, by land, and along the rivers, at the Lord’s command and by the king’s order, they dispersed to their respective places.

Those who had formerly been under the enemy’s hand now went about with the glory and splendor of authority, so that from then on no one could trouble them at all. They gathered all their individual goods and possessions according to the register, for everyone, in fear and trembling, brought out and handed over whatever belonging to anyone was in their possession, because of the deliverance wrought by the great God. Blessed is God, who rescues Israel from everything, from all afflictions and sorrows. To him be glory and honor and power, now and always and forever and ever. Amen. The Third Book of Maccabees is completed.
